slides.title: [1] Recall the provided formula — one Gaussian dip
slides.code:
import numpy as np

def basin(x: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray, cx: float,
          cy: float, depth: float, wx: float,
          wy: float) -> np.ndarray:
    """Gaussian dip of depth, centered at (cx, cy)."""
    dx = ((x - cx) ** 2) / (2 * wx ** 2)
    dy = ((y - cy) ** 2) / (2 * wy ** 2)
    return -depth * np.exp(-(dx + dy))

print(round(basin(0.40, 0.30, 0.52, 0.25,
                  30.0, 0.06, 0.18), 3))
slides.explainHead: Type the helper out in full
slides.explainBody: basin is the helper energy_proxy is built from — a smooth dip reaching its lowest value, -depth, exactly at (cx, cy) and fading back toward 0 away from it. A docstring plus type hints on every function is this course's convention from Week 4 onward, and your handout's copy is line-for-line the same as this one. At the baseline design (0.40, 0.30), this particular dip contributes only -3.906.
slides.teaching: Confirm every console prints exactly -3.906 before the next cell builds energy_proxy on top of it — a mismatch here means basin was retyped incorrectly, and every later sweep would inherit the error.

slides.title: ...continued: energy_proxy and the baseline design
slides.code:
def energy_proxy(v: tuple[float, float]) -> float:
    """Provided proxy to MINIMIZE; v=(wwr, shade_m)."""
    w, s = v
    base = 20.0
    b1 = basin(w, s, 0.52, 0.25, 30.0, 0.06, 0.18)
    b2 = basin(w, s, 0.28, 0.90, 34.0, 0.06, 0.18)
    ridge = 6.0 * np.exp(-((w - 0.40) ** 2) / 0.02)
    return base + b1 + b2 + ridge

baseline = energy_proxy((0.40, 0.30))
print(f'{baseline:.3f}')
slides.explainBody: energy_proxy is provided — you are not deriving it, only calling, sweeping, and visualizing it. Two basin calls place the two dips; ridge adds the soft wall near wwr=0.40. v=(wwr, shade_m) is a single packed input, the exact shape Week 11 will hand to scipy.optimize.minimize.
slides.teaching: Confirm every student's console prints exactly 22.076 before moving on — a mismatch here means the formula was retyped incorrectly.

slides.title: Vectorization, revisited
slides.definition: Applying one operation to an entire ndarray at once, with NumPy doing the looping internally — not a faster approximation, but the identical arithmetic as an explicit Python loop, just without writing the loop yourself.

example.head: Cell [2], next
example.body: wwr_check = np.linspace(0.20, 0.60, 21); vectorized = energy_proxy((wwr_check, 0.30)) runs all 21 values in one call. A loop over the same 21 values must match it exactly — np.allclose confirms that next.

slides.note: Vectorized code is not a different, approximate shortcut that happens to run faster — it is the exact same formula, applied to a whole array instead of one value at a time. Speed is a side effect, not the reason it is correct.
slides.teaching: Point back at Monday's list-vs-ndarray contrast before cell [2] runs — today's required assert is the proof that vectorized and looped truly agree, not just an assumption carried over from Monday.

slides.title: [2] REQUIRED: vectorized call vs. an explicit loop
slides.code:
wwr_check = np.linspace(0.20, 0.60, 21)

vectorized = energy_proxy((wwr_check, 0.30))

looped = []
for w in wwr_check:
    looped.append(energy_proxy((w, 0.30)))
looped = np.array(looped)

assert np.allclose(vectorized, looped)
print('vectorized == looped:', np.allclose(vectorized, looped))
slides.explainBody: 21 wwr values, computed two ways: once as one vectorized ndarray call, once as an explicit Python loop appending one call at a time. np.allclose confirms they are numerically identical — vectorization is the same arithmetic, not a different, faster-but-approximate shortcut. This assert is REQUIRED and graded.
slides.teaching: State plainly: every sweep for the rest of this studio depends on this exact equivalence holding. This is this week's required assert-verified check.

slides.title: Studio 2: explain why this assert matters before continuing
slides.prompt: The assert passed silently — say out loud why that silence is the point.
steps: Confirm the cell produced no AssertionError.
State what would print if vectorized and looped ever disagreed.
Name one reason a loop and a vectorized call could differ (floating-point order).
Explain why np.allclose, not ==, is the correct comparison here.
slides.teaching: Expected: == could fail on a last-bit floating-point difference even when the values are practically identical; allclose checks 'close enough,' the correct standard for numeric equivalence.

slides.title: Predict before cell [3] runs
slides.code:
wwr_vals = np.linspace(0.20, 0.60, 9)
shade_vals = np.linspace(0.0, 1.2, 9)

e_wwr = energy_proxy((wwr_vals, 0.30))
e_shade = energy_proxy((0.40, shade_vals))

print('wwr range:', round(e_wwr.max()-e_wwr.min(), 3))
print('shade range:', round(e_shade.max()-e_shade.min(), 3))
slides.question: Which range is bigger here: e_wwr's or e_shade's?
options: wwr's range will be clearly bigger
shade_m's range will be clearly bigger, since its bounds (0 to 1.2) span more raw distance
The two ranges will be about equal
Neither — both e_wwr and e_shade will be constant arrays
slides.why: Verified: e_wwr's range is 28.373 vs. e_shade's 3.46. Option B is the classic mix-up — wider bounds do not mean a wider output range.
slides.teaching: Let the room commit to an answer before cell [3] runs — option B's mistake (wider bounds must mean a wider effect) is common and worth naming even though it is wrong.

slides.title: [3] Sweep one variable at a time — first read
slides.code:
wwr_vals = np.linspace(0.20, 0.60, 9)
shade_vals = np.linspace(0.0, 1.2, 9)

e_wwr = energy_proxy((wwr_vals, 0.30))
e_shade = energy_proxy((0.40, shade_vals))

print('wwr range:', round(e_wwr.max()-e_wwr.min(), 3))
print('shade range:', round(e_shade.max()-e_shade.min(), 3))
slides.explainBody: wwr's range (28.373) dwarfs shade_m's range (3.46) at these two fixed baselines. Before reporting 'wwr is the important variable,' the next cell tests whether that survives a different choice of fixed baseline.
slides.teaching: Let the obvious conclusion form out loud before revealing it is incomplete — the next cell is the payoff, not a surprise sprung with no setup.

slides.title: Predict before cell [4] runs
slides.code:
e_shade2 = energy_proxy((0.28, shade_vals))
print('shade range @ wwr=0.28:',
      round(e_shade2.max()-e_shade2.min(), 3))

e_wwr2 = energy_proxy((wwr_vals, 0.90))
print('wwr range @ shade=0.90:',
      round(e_wwr2.max()-e_wwr2.min(), 3))
slides.question: Re-sweep at wwr=0.28, shade=0.90 — does the ranking hold?
options: Yes — shade_m's range stays small (roughly 3 to 4) no matter where wwr is fixed
No — shade_m's range grows past wwr's original 28.373
No — wwr's range shrinks to nearly zero
Yes — both ranges shrink together, since a baseline swap can only lower them
slides.why: Verified: shade range @ wwr=0.28 is 33.996 — bigger than wwr's own 28.373. A one-at-a-time sweep reports only the slice you fixed.
slides.teaching: This is the pivot of the whole studio — do not soften the reveal. Most students pick option A because cell [3]'s ranking felt conclusive.

slides.title: [4] The trap: re-run both sweeps from different baselines
slides.code:
e_shade2 = energy_proxy((0.28, shade_vals))
print('shade range @ wwr=0.28:',
      round(e_shade2.max()-e_shade2.min(), 3))

e_wwr2 = energy_proxy((wwr_vals, 0.90))
print('wwr range @ shade=0.90:',
      round(e_wwr2.max()-e_wwr2.min(), 3))
slides.output:
shade range @ wwr=0.28: 33.996
wwr range @ shade=0.90: 33.182
slides.explainHead: shade_m was never the less-important variable
slides.explainBody: Fixed at wwr=0.28 instead of 0.40, shade_m's own range jumps from 3.46 to 33.996 — bigger than wwr's original 28.373. Cell [3]'s conclusion was an artifact of where the other variable was fixed, not a fact about the formula.
slides.teaching: This is the exact trap from Monday's lecture, now reproduced on the students' own machines — confirm every console matches these two numbers before Studio 3.

slides.title: Studio 3: state why the first read was incomplete
slides.prompt: Cell [3] and cell [4] used the identical two sweeps — only the fixed baselines changed.
steps: Name the two ranges from cell [3] and the two from cell [4].
State which variable 'wins' under each pair of baselines.

slides.title: Boolean mask, revisited
slides.definition: An array of True/False values, one per element, built from a comparison like e_wwr <= target. Using that mask to index a DIFFERENT array of the SAME shape — wwr_vals[mask] — keeps only the elements where the condition holds.
slides.exampleLabel: Same shape is what makes it work

example.head: Cell [5], next
example.body: meets_target = e_wwr <= 15.0 builds one True/False per element of e_wwr. wwr_vals[meets_target] then reuses that exact mask on wwr_vals, a different array — because both share shape (9,). 4 of 9 wwr values pass.

slides.note: A mask only works on an array of the SAME shape it was built from. e_wwr's mask cannot be reused on the 81x61 meshgrid Z a few slides ahead — that grid needs its own comparison, built from Z itself.
slides.teaching: Connect back to Monday's & / | filtering on a pandas Series — this is the identical idea, one level closer to the raw array.

slides.title: [5] Boolean mask: flag which wwr values meet a target
slides.code:
target = 15.0
meets_target = e_wwr <= target

print(meets_target)
print('passing wwr values:', wwr_vals[meets_target])
slides.output:
[False False False False False  True  True  True  True]
passing wwr values: [0.45 0.5  0.55 0.6 ]
slides.explainHead: One shape, two arrays, one mask
slides.explainBody: e_wwr <= target compares all 9 values to 15.0 at once. wwr_vals[meets_target] then uses that same True/False array to pull matching wwr values out of a DIFFERENT array — 4 of 9 pass this target.
slides.teaching: Point out meets_target, e_wwr, and wwr_vals all share shape (9,) — that shared shape is exactly what makes cross-array masking work.

slides.title: Read the meshgrid call before you run it

parts.label: WW — grid of wwr values
parts.body: Shape (61, 81) — wwr_fine repeated down every row.

parts.label: SS — grid of shade_m values
parts.body: Shape (61, 81) — shade_fine repeated across every column.

parts.label: Builds every combination
parts.body: Turns two separate 1-D arrays into two full 2-D grids, ready for one vectorized formula call.

slides.teaching: Trace WW and SS's shape, (61, 81), back to wwr_fine (81 values) and shade_fine (61 values) before cell [6] runs — meshgrid orders shape as (length of the second array, length of the first).

slides.title: [6] Sweep both variables together with meshgrid
slides.code:
wwr_fine = np.linspace(0.20, 0.60, 81)
shade_fine = np.linspace(0.0, 1.2, 61)
WW, SS = np.meshgrid(wwr_fine, shade_fine)
Z = energy_proxy((WW, SS))
print('grid shape:', Z.shape, '=', Z.size, 'combinations')
best = np.unravel_index(np.argmin(Z), Z.shape)
print('grid best:', WW[best], SS[best], round(Z[best], 3))
print('local center:', round(energy_proxy((0.52, 0.25)), 3))
slides.output:
grid shape: (61, 81) = 4941 combinations
grid best: 0.275 0.9 -11.135
local center: -7.08
slides.explainBody: WW and SS both have shape (61, 81) — 4,941 (wwr, shade_m) pairs, every one of 81 wwr values crossed with every one of 61 shade_m values. Recall from Monday: np.argmin(Z) locates the smallest value in the flattened grid, and np.unravel_index converts that flat position back to (row, column) so WW[best]/SS[best] read the real wwr/shade_m. The best sampled point is -11.135 at (0.275, 0.900), clearly better than the other sampled basin near (0.52, 0.25). This dense 81 × 61 grid corroborates the better region; it does not prove the continuous global optimum.
slides.teaching: Name explicitly: same meshgrid technique as Monday's coarse 63-point demo, just finer linspace arrays — no new tool, only more points.

slides.title: argmin and unravel_index, defined
slides.definition: np.argmin(Z) returns the position of Z's smallest value, but flattened into one long index, as if the whole 2-D grid were a single row. np.unravel_index(pos, Z.shape) converts that flat position back into a (row, column) pair, so WW[row, col] and SS[row, col] read the real wwr and shade_m there.

example.head: best = np.unravel_index(np.argmin(Z), Z.shape)
example.body: WW[best] and SS[best] read the coordinates of the single smallest cell in the 4,941-point grid: 0.275, 0.900, with a sampled value of -11.135. That identifies the grid best, not a proof of the continuous global minimum.

slides.note: np.argmin alone returns one flat number (0 to 4940 here), not a (row, column) pair. Skipping unravel_index and using that number directly on WW would read the wrong cell.
slides.teaching: Walk this on the board with a small 2x3 example before trusting the real 61x81 grid — the flat-to-(row,column) conversion is the one new idea here, not a new kind of search.

slides.title: Three sweep strategies, same formula, compared
rows: No — flips at a new baseline
slides.callout: Neither one-at-a-time sweep was wrong about its own two numbers — each was simply incomplete. Evaluating every sampled combination together identifies which sampled region wins; the dense grid corroborates that region without proving a continuous global optimum.
slides.teaching: Point at each row in turn — this table compresses the whole studio's logic onto one slide, right before the heatmap makes it visible.

slides.title: [7] Visualize the full surface as a heatmap
slides.code:
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 5))
mesh = ax.pcolormesh(WW, SS, Z, cmap='RdYlGn_r', shading='auto')
fig.colorbar(mesh, ax=ax, label='energy_proxy (lower is better)')

ax.set_xlabel('wwr (window-to-wall ratio)')
ax.set_ylabel('shade_m (overhang depth, m)')
ax.set_title('energy_proxy(wwr, shade_m) -- full sweep')
fig.tight_layout()
fig.savefig('radley_energy_sweep_heatmap.png', dpi=150)
slides.explainBody: pcolormesh colors all 4,941 grid cells by energy_proxy. The deepest green pocket is upper-left (low wwr, high shade_m: the grid's best sampled basin); a shallower pocket is lower-right (higher wwr, low shade_m). A red ridge near wwr=0.40 separates them. The next slide shows the actual saved figure.
slides.teaching: Per course policy, no fabricated text output for a plotting call. Confirm this exact code runs cleanly against real matplotlib before class, and that both basins are visibly distinguishable at projector resolution.

slides.title: Studio 4: read the heatmap and write the required finding
slides.prompt: A heatmap is not yet a sensitivity finding until you can state it in one sentence.

State the grid best's (wwr, shade_m) and its energy_proxy value.

slides.title: [8] AI-audit: a plausible but flawed sensitivity script (1 of 2)
slides.code:
def ai_sweep_and_compare(energy_proxy):
    # audit target: two seeded defects
    wwr_vals = np.linspace(0.20, 0.60, 9)
    shade_vals = np.linspace(0.0, 1.2, 9)

    # "sweep both variables together"
    combined = energy_proxy((wwr_vals, shade_vals))
    print('combined shape:', combined.shape)
slides.explainBody: energy_proxy((wwr_vals, shade_vals)) with no meshgrid does not sweep 'both together' — NumPy pairs the two arrays elementwise, giving 9 diagonal pairs, not the 81 combinations a real grid needs. combined.shape prints (9,), not (9, 9) — the first tell.
slides.teaching: Give students exactly this much of the function and ask what combined.shape SHOULD print if both variables were truly swept together — (9, 9), not (9,) — before revealing bug 2 next.

slides.title: [8] AI-audit: a plausible but flawed sensitivity script (2 of 2)
slides.code:
# bug 2: shade swept at a mismatched wwr=0.60
    e_w = energy_proxy((wwr_vals, 0.30))
    e_s = energy_proxy((0.60, shade_vals))
    wwr_range = e_w.max() - e_w.min()
    shade_range = e_s.max() - e_s.min()
    print(f'wwr range: {wwr_range:.3f}')
    print(f'shade range: {shade_range:.3f}')
    if wwr_range > shade_range:
        print('Conclusion: wwr is more important.')
ai_sweep_and_compare(energy_proxy)
slides.output:
wwr range: 28.373
shade range: 11.867
Conclusion: wwr is more important.
slides.explainBody: wwr_range is measured at shade_m=0.30, while shade_range is measured at a DIFFERENT wwr=0.60 — exactly the one-at-a-time trap from cells [3]-[4]. Both bugs together produce a confident, wrong conclusion: 'wwr is more important.'
slides.teaching: Require students to name both defects, using cell [4]'s own 33.996 as counter-evidence, before Studio 5 asks them to rewrite and repair this exact function.

slides.title: Studio 5: diagnose and repair both defects
slides.prompt: Both bugs above run without any error message.
steps: Name the missing-meshgrid defect and what combined.shape should be instead.
Name the mismatched-baseline defect, citing cell [4]'s 33.996 as counter-evidence.
Rewrite ai_sweep_and_compare using meshgrid and matched baselines.

slides.title: Predict before cell [9] runs
slides.code:
strict_mask = Z <= -9.0
print('passing cells:', strict_mask.sum(), '/', Z.size)

region = (WW>=0.45)&(WW<=0.60)&(SS>=0.15)&(SS<=0.35)
local_min = np.min(np.where(region, Z, np.inf))
print('sub-region min:', round(local_min, 3))
slides.question: How many cells will strict_mask.sum() count?
options: About half the grid — roughly 2,470 cells
A small fraction — a few dozen cells
Zero — a continuous formula never lands exactly on a threshold
Nearly all of it — the lower basin dominates the grid
slides.why: 45 of 4,941 sampled cells—under 1%. The -9.0 target lies close to the best sampled value, so only a small neighborhood qualifies.
slides.teaching: The mask counts every sampled cell at or below -9.0, not only cells exactly equal to it.

slides.title: [9] Self-check: a stricter target and the other basin
slides.code:
strict_mask = Z <= -9.0
print('cells meeting target <=-9.0:', strict_mask.sum(),
      '/', Z.size)

region_local = (WW>=0.45)&(WW<=0.60)&(SS>=0.15)&(SS<=0.35)
local_min = np.min(np.where(region_local, Z, np.inf))
print('local sub-region grid minimum:', round(local_min, 3))
slides.output:
cells meeting target <=-9.0: 45 / 4941
local sub-region grid minimum: -7.103
slides.explainHead: Same tools, an unseen threshold and region
slides.explainBody: target=15.0 (cell [5]) becomes -9.0 here — much stricter, and it isolates only the better sampled basin's neighborhood (45 of 4,941 cells). Restricting to the other sampled basin's own sub-region finds a grid minimum of -7.103, matching the -7.08 direct-call value from cell [6] within grid resolution.
slides.teaching: This is the exact 'different threshold, different region' the plan's transfer safeguard requires — name it as such to students before Studio 6.

slides.title: Exit check: defend the sensitivity finding
slides.prompt: State your one-sentence finding from Studio 4, cold, no notes.
steps: Name the best (wwr, shade_m) region.
State its energy_proxy value and the improvement over baseline.
Name one reason a one-at-a-time sweep could have missed this region.
Be ready to explain it without looking at your script.
slides.teaching: Cold-call two volunteers. This rehearses the kind of question Week 11's multi-start comparison will ask about this exact same surface.

slides.title: One sweep, both variables, one honest sentence
takeaways: A vectorized ndarray call and an explicit loop must agree — assert it before trusting any sweep.
One-at-a-time sweeps can flip their own conclusion depending on where the other variable is fixed.
meshgrid evaluates every combination together — the only fair way to compare two variables.
The verified finding: aim near wwr=0.275, shade_m=0.90 — about 33.2 points better than baseline.
slides.teaching: Students save, restart the kernel, run from the top, and submit the script plus its heatmap PNG before Monday, 9:00am.
